# Measuring Things: Contexts and Units {#sec-contexts-units}

::: {.chapter-abstract}
Five records that say "millimetres, radians, and anything closer than a ten-millionth is the same point." Why a millimetre is three types at once, how an inch file smuggles in a millimetre anyway, and what a kernel's tolerance is doing in an exchange file.
:::

Every number in the geometry of the block file — the `60.` in a corner point, the `1.` in a direction, the `3.` in a circle's radius later on — is a bare real.
Nothing on the record says what unit it is in.
That information lives in one place, and every geometric representation points at it:

```step
#10 = ADVANCED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION('',(#11,#15),#165);
    ...
#165 = ( GEOMETRIC_REPRESENTATION_CONTEXT(3)
  GLOBAL_UNCERTAINTY_ASSIGNED_CONTEXT((#169))
  GLOBAL_UNIT_ASSIGNED_CONTEXT((#166,#167,#168))
  REPRESENTATION_CONTEXT('Context #1','3D Context with UNIT and UNCERTAINTY') );
#166 = ( LENGTH_UNIT() NAMED_UNIT(*) SI_UNIT(.MILLI.,.METRE.) );
#167 = ( NAMED_UNIT(*) PLANE_ANGLE_UNIT() SI_UNIT($,.RADIAN.) );
#168 = ( NAMED_UNIT(*) SI_UNIT($,.STERADIAN.) SOLID_ANGLE_UNIT() );
#169 = UNCERTAINTY_MEASURE_WITH_UNIT(LENGTH_MEASURE(1.E-07),#166,
  'distance_accuracy_value','confusion accuracy');
```

Read top down: *a three-dimensional coordinate space, measured in millimetres, radians and steradians, in which two points closer than $10^{-7}$ mm are the same point.*

## Representations and their contexts {#sec-contexts-units-representations}

The word *representation* is Part 43's, and it is worth a moment because it organises half the file.
A **representation** is a bag of **representation items** together with a **representation context** that says how to interpret them.
`#10` is a representation: its items are `#11` (an axis placement) and `#15` (a solid), and its context is `#165`.
Every point, curve, surface, face and solid in the file is a representation item, and every one belongs to some representation, and every representation has exactly one context.

The context is where units live.
It is shared: in a single-part file one context carries the units and every geometric representation points at it — though the file may still hold a unitless 2D context per pcurve, as @sec-pcurves-meshes shows.
In an assembly file there may be several — OCCT writes one per product, all identical — and each representation points at its own.
A reader that assumes one context per file will be right most of the time and wrong in ways that are hard to notice.

## The context record {#sec-contexts-units-context-record}

`#165` is a complex instance of four types, and @sec-schema explained why: `representation_context` has no supertype constraint, so any combination of its subtypes is legal, and this one is three at once.

- `REPRESENTATION_CONTEXT('Context #1','3D Context with UNIT and UNCERTAINTY')` — the root, with an identifier and a free-text type.
  Both strings are the writer's choice and mean nothing to a reader.
- `GEOMETRIC_REPRESENTATION_CONTEXT(3)` — this context is for geometry, in three dimensions.
  Two-dimensional contexts, `(2)`, appear in files that carry drawing views or the 2D parameter-space curves of @sec-pcurves-meshes.
- `GLOBAL_UNIT_ASSIGNED_CONTEXT((#166,#167,#168))` — the units in force for every item in this context.
- `GLOBAL_UNCERTAINTY_ASSIGNED_CONTEXT((#169))` — the tolerance in force.

AP214 requires the unit set to hold exactly one length unit and exactly one plane angle unit; AP203 and AP242 leave the combination to the recommended practices.
It says nothing about solid angle.
Nothing in a mechanical file ever measures one either, but exporters write a steradian anyway, so you will see `#168` in nearly every file.

## The millimetre {#sec-contexts-units-millimetre}

```step
#166 = ( LENGTH_UNIT() NAMED_UNIT(*) SI_UNIT(.MILLI.,.METRE.) );
```

Three blocks, alphabetical.
`LENGTH_UNIT()` declares no attributes and says only *this measures length*.
`NAMED_UNIT(*)` carries the derived `dimensions`.
`SI_UNIT(.MILLI.,.METRE.)` gives the prefix and the base unit.
A metre would be `SI_UNIT($,.METRE.)`; a micron `SI_UNIT(.MICRO.,.METRE.)`.
The radian and steradian at `#167` and `#168` follow the same pattern with `$` for no prefix, and with `PLANE_ANGLE_UNIT()` and `SOLID_ANGLE_UNIT()` in place of `LENGTH_UNIT()`.

This exact record — the millimetre as a three-way complex instance — is probably the most frequently written line in all of STEP.

## Inch files {#sec-contexts-units-inch-files}

Imperial units cannot be spelled with an SI prefix and name, so an inch is a **conversion-based unit**: a named unit defined as a multiple of another unit.
The block, exported by the same OCCT build with its output unit set to inches:

```step
#166 = ( CONVERSION_BASED_UNIT('INCH',#168) LENGTH_UNIT() NAMED_UNIT(#167) );
#167 = DIMENSIONAL_EXPONENTS(1.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.);
#168 = LENGTH_MEASURE_WITH_UNIT(25.4,#169);
#169 = ( LENGTH_UNIT() NAMED_UNIT(*) SI_UNIT(.MILLI.,.METRE.) );
#172 = UNCERTAINTY_MEASURE_WITH_UNIT(LENGTH_MEASURE(3.937007874016E-09),#166,
  'distance_accuracy_value','confusion accuracy');
```

`#166` is still a length unit and still a named unit, but `SI_UNIT` has been replaced by `CONVERSION_BASED_UNIT`, which carries a `name` and a `conversion_factor`.
Because the blocks are alphabetical it now sorts first.
The factor, `#168`, is a *measure with unit*: 25.4 of unit `#169`.
And `#169` is the millimetre.
So an inch file contains the millimetre after all — as the thing the inch is defined in terms of — and every coordinate in the file is then in inches: the block's far corner is at `(2.362204724409,0.787401574803,0.393700787402)`, and the uncertainty has been converted too, to $3.9 \times 10^{-9}$ inches.

Three details.
First, `NAMED_UNIT(#167)` is an explicit reference where the SI record had `*`.
An SI unit's dimensions are always derived from its name, so that slot is `*`.
For a conversion-based unit AP203 and AP242 require the exponents to be written out and to agree with the factor's unit, which is what this file does; AP214 edition 3 derives them instead, so a file written to that edition would carry `NAMED_UNIT(*)` and no `DIMENSIONAL_EXPONENTS` record.
Here `DIMENSIONAL_EXPONENTS(1.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.)` says length$^{1}$ mass$^{0}$ time$^{0}$ current$^{0}$ temperature$^{0}$ substance$^{0}$ luminosity$^{0}$ — a length.
Second, the string `'INCH'` is a label.
What makes it an inch is the `25.4`.
A reader that keys on the name will meet `'inch'`, `'IN'` and `'Inch'` before long; the factor is the reliable part.
Third — and this is a real defect in a widely used exporter — the `25.4` in `#168` is written bare.
@sec-schema's rule says a SELECT-typed value that is not an entity must be wrapped, and the uncertainty record two lines below wraps its value correctly as `LENGTH_MEASURE(...)`; the conversion factor should read `LENGTH_MEASURE(25.4)`.
Every mainstream reader accepts the bare form, which is why it has never been fixed, and it is a fair specimen of the gap between the standard and the files.

Angles are treated the same way.
A file that measures angles in degrees carries (this excerpt written to the same pattern rather than exported)

```step
#900 = ( CONVERSION_BASED_UNIT('DEGREE',#901) NAMED_UNIT(#902)
         PLANE_ANGLE_UNIT() );
#901 = PLANE_ANGLE_MEASURE_WITH_UNIT(PLANE_ANGLE_MEASURE(0.01745329252),#903);
#902 = DIMENSIONAL_EXPONENTS(0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.);
#903 = ( NAMED_UNIT(*) PLANE_ANGLE_UNIT() SI_UNIT($,.RADIAN.) );
```

— a degree is 0.0174533 radians, and an angle is dimensionless, so every exponent is zero.

## Uncertainty {#sec-contexts-units-uncertainty}

```step
#169 = UNCERTAINTY_MEASURE_WITH_UNIT(LENGTH_MEASURE(1.E-07),#166,
  'distance_accuracy_value','confusion accuracy');
```

Four attributes: a value (wrapped, because `measure_value` is a SELECT), a unit (bare, because it is an entity), a name, and a description.
The name is the important one.
`'distance_accuracy_value'` is the string the recommended practices call for, and it means: *two points closer together than this value are to be treated as coincident.*
Here that is one ten-millionth of a millimetre.

::: {.callout-note title="Engineering background: Why a tolerance travels with the geometry"}
A boundary representation says that a solid's faces meet along shared edges and its edges meet at shared vertices.
But the faces are defined by surfaces — planes, cylinders, splines — and the edges by curves, and those are computed in floating point.
Where a cylinder meets a plane, the curve of intersection does not lie *exactly* on either; it lies within some small distance of both.
Whether a shell is "closed" is therefore a question about a threshold: are the gaps smaller than the tolerance?
Every geometric kernel has such a threshold, and they differ — $10^{-7}$ in Open CASCADE, $10^{-6}$ or $10^{-8}$ elsewhere, sometimes scaled to the model's size.
The file records the writer's value so that a reader can know how tightly the geometry was made to fit.
If the reader's kernel is stricter, gaps that were invisible at export become holes at import, and the solid falls apart into a surface model.
Much of the "healing" that STEP importers do is repairing exactly that.
:::

The uncertainty is what makes the same file behave differently in different tools.
A `'confusion accuracy'` of $10^{-7}$ mm from one kernel and $10^{-4}$ mm from another describe geometry of very different quality, and the reader that ignores this value is the one whose imports mysteriously fail.

## Derived units {#sec-contexts-units-derived-units}

Length, angle and solid angle cover geometry.
Properties such as area, volume and mass need units that are products of the base ones, and Part 41 provides `DERIVED_UNIT`:

```step
#300 = DERIVED_UNIT((#301));
#301 = DERIVED_UNIT_ELEMENT(#166,3.);
```

`#300` is "millimetres to the power three" — a cubic millimetre — built from one element: the length unit `#166` raised to the exponent `3.`.
An area would use `2.`; a density would combine a mass unit with exponent `1.` and a length unit with exponent `-3.`.
These appear with validation properties in @sec-properties-validation and almost nowhere else.

## Contexts in assemblies {#sec-contexts-units-assemblies}

The clamp assembly of @sec-assemblies has three geometric contexts, one per product, all textually identical to `#165`.
Each product's shape representation points at its own.
This is not merely common but forced: the transformation record that places a component requires its two representations to sit in different context records, so an assembly written that way cannot share one.
It has a consequence that is easy to state and easy to forget: **units are a property of the representation, not of the file.**
A file may, in principle, hold one part in millimetres and another in inches, each in its own context, and an assembly that places both.
Readers that read the first context they find and apply it to everything will get the second part wrong by a factor of 25.4.
Follow the reference from each representation to its context; never cache "the" unit.

::: {.callout-important title="In brief"}
Units live in the representation context, which every geometric representation references.
A geometric context carries a length unit and a plane angle unit — required by AP214, conventional elsewhere — and by convention a solid angle unit too; each is a complex instance.
SI units derive their dimensions; conversion-based units (inch, degree) state them and define themselves as a multiple of an SI unit, so inch files contain the millimetre.
The uncertainty is the writing kernel's coincidence tolerance, named `'distance_accuracy_value'`.
A file can have several contexts; units belong to representations, not files.
:::
